anatomy.q: Structures develop from the 3rd pharyngeal pouch
anatomy.a: Inferior parathyroid glands and the thymus

anatomy.q: What adult structure is the remnant of the fetal umbilical vein?
anatomy.a: Ligamentum teres hepatis (round ligament of the liver)

anatomy.q: Damage to the common fibular (peroneal) nerve at the neck of the fibula leads to which classic gait abnormality?
anatomy.a: Foot drop (steppage gait) due to loss of dorsiflexion and eversion.

anatomy.q: Nerve injured in mid-shaft humerus fracture, causing wrist drop?
Nerve compressed in carpal tunnel syndrome?
Claw hand follows injury to which nerve?

anatomy.a: C5 and C6 (upper trunk); waiter's tip position

anatomy.q: Root value of the phrenic nerve?
Cranial nerve with the longest intracranial course?
Cranial nerve supplying the lateral rectus?
anatomy.a: Abducens (VI). Rule: LR6 SO4, rest by 3

anatomy.q: At which vertebral level does the trachea bifurcate into the left and right main bronchi (the carina)?
Through which skull foramen does the middle meningeal artery enter the cranial cavity?
anatomy.a: Foramen spinosum (laceration from a pterion fracture causes an epidural hematoma).
Lenticulostriate branch of the middle cerebral artery

anatomy.q: Which ligament supports the ovary and carries the ovarian vessels?

anatomy.a: Junction of lateral one-third and medial two-thirds of the line from ASIS to umbilicus

anatomy.q: Level of the three diaphragm openings?

physiology.q: Which receptors mediate the baroreceptor reflex in the aortic arch and carotid sinus, and which cranial nerves carry their afferent signals?
physiology.a: Stretch mechanoreceptors; carried by the vagus nerve (CN X) from the aortic arch and the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) from the carotid sinus.

physiology.q: cells in the gastric mucosa secrete hydrochloric acid (HCl) and intrinsic factor
physiology.a: Parietal (oxyntic) cells (intrinsic factor is required for vitamin B₁₂ absorption in the terminal ileum).

physiology.q: Natural pacemaker of the heart?
physiology.a: Sinoatrial (SA) node, which has the fastest intrinsic rate

physiology.q: hypothalamic nucleus acts as the master circadian pacemaker of the body
physiology.a: Suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) (regulates melatonin release from the pineal gland)

physiology.q: Which clotting factors are vitamin K-dependent, and where are they synthesized?
physiology.a: Factors II, VII, IX, X, plus Protein C and Protein S; synthesized in the liver via gamma-carboxylation.

physiology.q: How does insulin regulate blood glucose levels in skeletal muscle and adipose tissue?
physiology.a: Promotes GLUT4 transporter translocation to the cell membrane, increasing glucose uptake, glycogenesis, lipogenesis, and protein synthesis.

physiology.q: Ascending spinal tract carries pain and temperature sensation, and where does it decussate?
physiology.a: Lateral spinothalamic tract; decussates within 1–2 spinal segments via the anterior white commissure.

physiology.q: Normal glomerular filtration rate?
physiology.a: About 125 mL/min

physiology.q: Site of erythropoietin production?
physiology.a: Kidney (peritubular interstitial cells)

physiology.q: Hormones released from the posterior pituitary?
physiology.a: ADH (vasopressin) and oxytocin, made in the hypothalamus

physiology.q: Function and source of surfactant?
physiology.a: Lowers alveolar surface tension; secreted by type II pneumocytes

physiology.q: Normal tidal volume?
physiology.a: About 500 mL

physiology.q: Normal vital capacity (adult male)?
physiology.a: About 4 to 5 litres

physiology.q: Normal pH of arterial blood?
Ion that triggers muscle contraction by binding troponin C?
physiology.a: Calcium

physiology.q: Neurotransmitter at the neuromuscular junction?
physiology.a: Acetylcholine

physiology.q: Resting membrane potential of a neuron?
physiology.a: About -70 mV (skeletal muscle about -90 mV)

physiology.q: Cells that secrete HCl in the stomach?
physiology.a: Parietal (oxyntic) cells

physiology.q: Main site of nutrient absorption?
physiology.a: Small intestine (mainly jejunum); iron in duodenum, B12 in terminal ileum

physiology.q: Hormone that lowers blood glucose?
physiology.a: Insulin, from beta cells of the islets of Langerhans

Which lipoprotein is called bad cholesterol?
Which lipoprotein is called good cholesterol and why?
biochemistry.a: HDL; it carries cholesterol back to the liver

psychology.q: Piaget's four stages of cognitive development?
psychology.a: Sensorimotor, preoperational, concrete operational, formal operational
